title: Stoichiometry, Molar Mass & Limiting Reagents
summary: Converting mass to moles (n = m/M) and using balanced coefficients to identify the limiting reactant.

learningObjectives: Convert between mass in grams and amount in moles using n = m / M
Use stoichiometric mole ratios from balanced chemical equations
Identify the limiting reagent that governs maximum theoretical product yield
explanationSequence: Step 1: The Mole Bridge (n = m / M)
commonMisconceptions: Comparing reactant masses directly in grams instead of converting to moles first
Forgetting to divide moles by the stoichiometric coefficient when testing which reactant runs out first
instructions.socraticSystemPrompt: You are orchestrating the Stoichiometry lesson. Insist that students convert grams to moles before comparing reactants across a chemical equation.

resources.title: Stoichiometric Conversion Workflow
resources.bodyText:
• Moles: n = mass (g) / Molar Mass M (g/mol)
• Reaction Ratio (aA + bB → cC): n_A / a = n_B / b = n_C / c
• Limiting Reagent: The reactant with the smallest (n_available / coefficient) ratio.

resources.bodyText: In the balanced equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, coefficients represent mole ratios: 2 moles of hydrogen gas react with 1 mole of oxygen gas to form 2 moles of water.

resources.title: Animated Concept Walkthrough: Stoichiometry, Molar Mass & Limiting Reagents
resources.summary: 12-second teacher-curated animated walkthrough covering Steps 1–3 of Stoichiometry, Molar Mass & Limiting Reagents.
resources.bodyText:
Step 1 (Converting Mass to Moles (n = m / M)): To compare substances in a reaction, convert mass in grams to moles using n = m / M, where M is the molar mass in grams per mole.

Step 2 (Stoichiometric Mole Ratios): In the balanced equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, coefficients represent mole ratios: 2 moles of hydrogen gas react with 1 mole of oxygen gas to form 2 moles of water.

Step 3 (Determining the Limiting Reagent): When 4 moles of H₂ are mixed with 3 moles of O₂ in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, compare n/coeff: for H₂ it is 4/2 = 2, and for O₂ it is 3/1 = 3. H₂ is smaller, so H₂ is the limiting reagent.

objects.label: The Mole Bridge
objects.explanation: Chemical equations count molecules (moles), not grams. Divide mass m by molar mass M to enter the mole domain.

objects.label: Balanced Mole Ratio
objects.explanation: Every 2 moles of H₂ require exactly 1 mole of O₂ to produce 2 moles of H₂O.

objects.label: Limiting Reagent Test
objects.explanation: The reactant that runs out first stops the reaction and sets the maximum theoretical yield.

steps.title: Converting Mass to Moles (n = m / M)
steps.narration: To compare substances in a reaction, convert mass in grams to moles using n = m / M, where M is the molar mass in grams per mole.
steps.tutorTip: Tap 'The Mole Bridge' on the board to inspect the conversion formula.

inlineQuiz.question: Given the molar mass of Water (H₂O) is 18 g/mol, how many moles are in 54 g of water?
inlineQuiz.explanation: n = m / M = 54 g / 18 g/mol = 3.0 mol.

steps.title: Stoichiometric Mole Ratios
steps.narration: In the balanced equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, coefficients represent mole ratios: 2 moles of hydrogen gas react with 1 mole of oxygen gas to form 2 moles of water.
steps.tutorTip: Use the ratio (target coefficient / known coefficient) to scale moles.

inlineQuiz.question: In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of H₂ are needed to completely react with 2 moles of N₂?
inlineQuiz.explanation: Each mole of N₂ requires 3 moles of H₂, so 2 mol N₂ × 3 = 6 moles of H₂.

steps.title: Determining the Limiting Reagent
steps.narration: When 4 moles of H₂ are mixed with 3 moles of O₂ in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, compare n/coeff: for H₂ it is 4/2 = 2, and for O₂ it is 3/1 = 3. H₂ is smaller, so H₂ is the limiting reagent.
steps.tutorTip: Always compute product yield from the limiting reagent, never the excess reagent.

inlineQuiz.question: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, if you react 4 moles of H₂ with 3 moles of O₂, how many moles of H₂O are produced?
inlineQuiz.explanation: H₂ is limiting (4 mol H₂ consumes 2 mol O₂) and yields 4 moles of H₂O (1 mol O₂ remains in excess).
